title: "Async Programming with tokio"

# Async Programming with tokio

When a CLI application must query hundreds of HTTP endpoints, scrape multiple Git repositories in parallel, or monitor multiple file descriptor events simultaneously, synchronous I/O creates severe bottlenecks. `tokio` delivers an asynchronous runtime capable of driving millions of concurrent tasks with minimal CPU overhead.

## Configuring the Tokio Runtime for CLI Applications

In `Cargo.toml`:

```toml
[dependencies]
tokio = { version = "1.38", features = ["full"] }
reqwest = { version = "0.12", features = ["json"] }
futures = "0.3"
```

## The `#[tokio::main]` Attribute

The `#[tokio::main]` macro sets up the multi-threaded asynchronous executor and starts the root future:

```rust
use anyhow::Result;
use reqwest::Client;
use std::time::Duration;

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let client = Client::builder()
        .timeout(Duration::from_secs(5))
        .build()?;

    let response = client
        .get("https://httpbin.org/status/200")
        .send()
        .await?;

    println!("Async response status: {}", response.status());
    Ok(())
}
```

## Bounded Concurrency with `tokio::sync::Semaphore`

A common CLI mistake is launching thousands of unbounded concurrent network tasks, exhausting local socket descriptors or triggering remote rate limits (HTTP 429). Use a `Semaphore` to bound concurrent flight:

```rust
use std::sync::Arc;
use tokio::sync::Semaphore;
use anyhow::Result;

async fn fetch_urls(urls: Vec<String>) -> Result<()> {
    let client = reqwest::Client::new();
    // Allow at most 10 concurrent HTTP requests
    let semaphore = Arc::new(Semaphore::new(10));
    let mut handles = Vec::new();

    for url in urls {
        let permit = semaphore.clone().acquire_owned().await?;
        let client = client.clone();

        handles.push(tokio::spawn(async move {
            let res = client.get(&url).send().await;
            drop(permit); // Release slot for next request
            (url, res.map(|r| r.status()))
        }));
    }

    for handle in handles {
        let (url, result) = handle.await?;
        println!("{url} -> {:?}", result);
    }

    Ok(())
}
```

## Graceful Cancellation via `tokio::select!`

Listen for OS interrupt signals (`Ctrl+C`) while long-running network or disk jobs are active:

```rust
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    tokio::select! {
        _ = tokio::signal::ctrl_c() => {
            eprintln!("\nReceived Ctrl+C, gracefully terminating worker tasks...");
        }
        res = run_worker() => {
            println!("Worker completed with: {:?}", res);
        }
    }
}

async fn run_worker() -> Result<(), ()> {
    tokio::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(60)).await;
    Ok(())
}
```
